cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica), often single-village or old-tree maocha
processing: Raw pu-erh maocha is steamed briefly and hand-rolled or moulded into a tight ball of 5–8 g, dried, and usually wrapped individually in paper; the material is ordinary sheng, the form is the novelty.
harvest_season: Rolled from spring or autumn maocha and sold with that harvest year; most are made within months of picking.
appearance_dry: A tight, slightly knobbly dark-green sphere the size of a large marble, with silver buds showing on the surface.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold, clearing as the ball opens; a touch hazy in the first steep.
appearance_wet: The ball unfolds over several steeps into a nest of long, whole yellow-green leaves.
taste_profile: Whatever village went into it, released slowly: honey and florals that build over the first three steeps, a clean bitterness that softens as the ball opens, and a long sweet session once it is fully unfurled.

brewing.notes: Rinse twice, the second rinse for 20–30 seconds, to loosen the ball; or simply treat the first steep as a long one. One ball per 100–120 ml. Do not pry it apart; let it open on its own over the first three infusions.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year and village, usually in bags or tins of individually wrapped balls, and nearly always young: the form became common around 2012–2015 as a convenience format for Western and gift markets, so there is little mid-aged dragon-ball tea and no aged tradition at all. Because the ball is tightly compressed it changes more slowly than a loose cake, which is fine for tea meant to be drunk within a few years. Buy them for convenience and sampling; a 7–8 g ball from a famous village is often the cheapest way to taste that village's maocha.
description:
Dragon balls are raw pu-erh rolled into single-session spheres of around 7–8 g, and they are a thoroughly modern format: barely seen before the 2010s, now everywhere, because they solve the beginner's biggest problem with pu-erh, which is prying a cake without turning it to dust. One ball, one gaiwan, no knife.

The tea is ordinary sheng maocha, often from good single-village or old-tree lots, given a quick steam and rolled by hand into a tight ball that is dried and wrapped in a twist of paper. Compression is high, so the ball changes more slowly than loose leaf and opens more slowly in the cup.

That opening is the whole technique. Give it two rinses, the second a long one, or treat the first steep as a thirty-second warm-up; the ball will unfold over three infusions into a nest of whole leaves, and the session only really starts then. Do not pull it apart. Once open it tastes exactly like the maocha it was made from, honey and florals or Bulang bitterness as the case may be, for ten steeps or more.

They are sold by harvest year and village in bags and tins, by weight or by count, and they are an excellent sampling format: a bag of mixed villages is a cheap tasting flight. The caveats are that the ball hides the leaf, so grade and breakage are hard to judge, and that unusually cheap balls are usually made from broken or lower-grade maocha. Shu versions exist and are even more common as gifts.

They travel well, brew well in an office mug with a strainer, and are a kind way to introduce someone to sheng without handing them a cake and a pick.
